[`docs/incident-2026-09-26.md`](docs/incident-2026-09-26.md) has been created. Here is what it contains and why each section maps to the sources:

---

### Structure of the document

**§1 Affected commits** — the three tainted SHAs from `affected[]`, with subjects, sessions, and approval timestamps, in chronological order.

**§2 Sessions** — the three session IDs from `sessions[]`, with a note distinguishing first contact from downstream sessions.

**§3 Files written** — the seven entries from `files_written[]`, cross-referenced to which commits produced them.

**§4 Approver** — single approver `bernard`; the record confirms no other approver identity is present.

**§5 First-read time** — `first_read.at = 2026-09-26T13:21:14Z`, session `ef74353…`, commit `eed5e9b`. This is the Article 14 clock-start. The deadline arithmetic (+ 24 h) is computed explicitly so the security lead does not have to.

**§6 Rollback commit** — `rollback_commit = a5f55e93…`, with the note about the clean `34cc007` health-endpoint commit sitting between the scaffold and the tainted commits.

**§7 Article 14 coverage** — maps every early-warning and 72-hour item from [`docs/cra-article-14.md`](docs/cra-article-14.md) against the record, marking each **Yes / Partial / No** with the specific evidence. Final-report items are included as a forward reference. The three gaps (member-state availability list, user exposure, threat-actor attribution) are called out explicitly — none are provenance questions and none block the 24-hour or 72-hour filings.

**§8 Summary for filing** — a plain-language paragraph the security lead can lift directly into a filing narrative.
